lead: The sampling theorem of the first chapter is the low-pass sampling theorem: a signal from 0 to fmax needs fs > 2fmax. A signal that occupies only a band from fL to fH, with nothing near zero, can be sampled far below 2fH, because the empty space below fL gives the copies room. Real samplers also take samples of finite width, and a held sample flattens the top of the band: that droop is the aperture effect. Radio receivers use band-pass sampling; every practical converter has to live with the aperture effect.
prereq: You need: the repeated spectrum from sampling theorem and reconstruction and the folding rule from aliasing and anti-aliasing filters, plus the Fourier transform of a rectangular pulse (see Fourier transform of aperiodic signals).

sections.h3: Band-pass sampling: use the empty gaps

blocks.text: Let a real signal have energy only between fL and fH, with bandwidth B = fH − fL. Sampling repeats the band (and its mirror image at negative frequencies) every fs. The copies do not overlap if the whole band fits inside one Nyquist zone, a strip of width fs/2 between (m − 1)fs/2 and mfs/2 for some integer m. Writing that condition for both band edges gives the band-pass sampling theorem:
Here m is an integer with 1 ≤ m ≤ ⌊f<sub>H</sub>/B⌋. Each allowed m gives a range of valid rates; m = 1 is the low-pass case f<sub>s</sub> ≥ 2f<sub>H</sub>.

The largest m gives the lowest rate, f<sub>s</sub> = 2f<sub>H</sub>/m, which equals 2B when f<sub>H</sub> is an exact multiple of B. At the ends of a range the copies touch, with no guard band, so a real design picks a rate inside a range. A band in an odd zone (m odd) lands near zero the right way round; in an even zone it lands mirrored, with high and low frequencies swapped. To rebuild the original signal, filter the samples with a band-pass filter from f<sub>L</sub> to f<sub>H</sub>; for digital processing, the copy near zero already holds all the information.

A real sampler cannot take an impulse. Natural sampling multiplies x(t) by a train of narrow pulses of width τ, so each pulse top follows the signal. Its spectrum is a set of copies of X(f) at kfs with constant weights (τ/Ts) sinc(kτ/Ts): each copy keeps its shape, and a low-pass filter still recovers x(t) exactly.

Flat-top sampling, done by a sample-and-hold circuit, holds each sample value constant for τ seconds. The held train is the impulse train convolved with a rectangle of width τ, so its spectrum is Xs(f) multiplied by the rectangle's transform:

blocks.where: Here τ is the hold time in s, f the frequency in Hz and sinc(u) = sin(πu)/(πu). The factor e<sup>−jπfτ</sup> is a delay of τ/2; it changes no amplitude.

blocks.text: The magnitude |sinc(fτ)| is 1 at 0 Hz, falls across the band and reaches zero at f = 1/τ. This frequency-dependent loss is the aperture effect: unlike natural sampling, the baseband copy itself is distorted. For a full-period hold (τ = Ts, the zero-order hold used to drive a DAC), the gain at fs/2 is sinc(0.5) = 2/π ≈ 0.637, about −3.9 dB.

Two remedies are used. Make τ small compared with Ts, so that fτ stays near zero across the band. Or follow the hold with an equalizer of gain 1/|sinc(fτ)| over the signal band, often called an inverse-sinc filter. The equalizer also boosts noise near the band edge, so it is used only up to fmax. The held values are then rounded to a fixed number of levels, which is the next chapter, quantization of sampled signals.

examples.question: A signal has components only between 5 kHz and 6 kHz. Find every range of valid sampling rates, the lowest rate, and a practical rate with a guard band. For the practical rate, find where the band lands between 0 and f<sub>s</sub>/2.
steps: f<sub>L</sub> = 5 kHz, f<sub>H</sub> = 6 kHz, B = 1 kHz, so m runs from 1 to ⌊6/1⌋ = 6. Low-pass sampling would need f<sub>s</sub> > 2f<sub>H</sub> = 12 kHz.
Ranges 2f<sub>H</sub>/m ≤ f<sub>s</sub> ≤ 2f<sub>L</sub>/(m − 1): m = 2 gives 6 to 10 kHz; m = 3 gives 4 to 5 kHz; m = 4 gives 3 to 3.33 kHz; m = 5 gives 2.4 to 2.5 kHz; m = 6 gives 2 to 2 kHz.
Lowest rate: m = 6 gives f<sub>s</sub> = 12/6 = 2 kHz = 2B, but only that single value works, with the copies touching at both edges.
Practical rate: take m = 5 and f<sub>s</sub> = 2.45 kHz, inside 2.4 to 2.5 kHz. Zone 5 runs from 4 × 2.45/2 = 4.9 kHz to 5 × 2.45/2 = 6.125 kHz, and 5 to 6 kHz lies inside it.
The band lands at 5 − 2 × 2.45 = 0.1 kHz to 6 − 4.9 = 1.1 kHz, inside 0 to f<sub>s</sub>/2 = 1.225 kHz, the right way round because m = 5 is odd.
Margins: 0.1 kHz below the band image and 1.225 − 1.1 = 0.125 kHz above it.
examples.answer: Valid ranges are 6–10, 4–5, 3–3.33, 2.4–2.5 kHz and exactly 2 kHz. The lowest rate is 2 kHz (no margin); 2.45 kHz is a practical choice, and the band then appears at 0.1–1.1 kHz, against 12 kHz for low-pass sampling.

examples.question: Speech up to 3.4 kHz is sampled at 8 kHz with flat-top pulses. Find the aperture gain at 3.4 kHz and the equalizer gain needed there (a) for a full-period hold τ = T<sub>s</sub>, (b) for τ = 10 μs.
steps: Equalizer gain at 3.4 kHz = 1/0.728 = 1.37, a boost of 2.75 dB.
So a pulse 10 μs wide, 8% of the period, makes the aperture effect negligible.
examples.answer: (a) Gain 0.728 (−2.75 dB), equalizer gain 1.37 at 3.4 kHz. (b) Gain 0.998 (−0.017 dB), no equalizer needed.

traps: Rejecting a valid band-pass rate because it is below 2f<sub>H</sub>. The low-pass condition is not the band-pass condition.
Taking f<sub>s</sub> = 2B and stopping there. It works only when f<sub>H</sub> is a multiple of B, and even then the copies touch; check 2f<sub>H</sub>/m ≤ f<sub>s</sub> ≤ 2f<sub>L</sub>/(m − 1).
Saying natural sampling causes the aperture effect. Natural sampling only scales each copy; flat-top (sample-and-hold) sampling distorts the band.
Confusing the hold time τ with the sampling period T<sub>s</sub>. The first zero of sinc(fτ) is at 1/τ, which is f<sub>s</sub> only for a full-period hold.
Forgetting that 0.637 at f<sub>s</sub>/2 is for τ = T<sub>s</sub>; at the top of a real signal band (below f<sub>s</sub>/2) the droop is smaller.

quiz.q: State the low-pass and the band-pass sampling conditions.
quiz.a: Low-pass: f<sub>s</sub> > 2f<sub>max</sub>. Band-pass: 2f<sub>H</sub>/m ≤ f<sub>s</sub> ≤ 2f<sub>L</sub>/(m − 1) for an integer m with 1 ≤ m ≤ ⌊f<sub>H</sub>/B⌋, where B = f<sub>H</sub> − f<sub>L</sub>.

quiz.q: Why can a band-pass signal be sampled below 2f<sub>H</sub>?
quiz.a: The spectrum from 0 to f<sub>L</sub> is empty. The copies repeat every f<sub>s</sub>, and with the right rate they fall into that empty space without overlapping the band or each other.

quiz.q: A signal occupies 20 kHz to 24 kHz. Find the lowest valid band-pass rate.
quiz.a: B = 4 kHz, ⌊24/4⌋ = 6, so m = 6 and f<sub>s</sub> = 2 × 24/6 = 8 kHz. Upper limit 2f<sub>L</sub>/(m − 1) = 40/5 = 8 kHz, so 8 kHz is valid, with no margin.

quiz.q: A 7–9 kHz band is sampled at 4 kHz, which equals 2B. Show that the copies overlap.
quiz.a: Zones have width f<sub>s</sub>/2 = 2 kHz: 6–8, 8–10 kHz. The band 7–9 kHz straddles 8 kHz, so it does not fit in one zone. In the formula, m can be at most ⌊9/2⌋ = 4, and m = 4 needs f<sub>s</sub> ≥ 18/4 = 4.5 kHz (lower m needs even more), so 4 kHz is not allowed.

quiz.q: A full-period hold runs at f<sub>s</sub> = 8 kHz. Find the aperture gain at 4 kHz and at 2 kHz.
quiz.a: τ = 125 μs. At 4 kHz, fτ = 0.5 and the gain is 2/π ≈ 0.637. At 2 kHz, fτ = 0.25 and the gain is sin(π/4)/(π/4) ≈ 0.900.

quiz.q: What is the difference between natural and flat-top sampling?
quiz.a: Natural sampling keeps the signal shape on each pulse top; its spectrum copies are only scaled. Flat-top sampling holds a constant value; the spectrum is multiplied by τ sinc(fτ), which droops at high frequency (the aperture effect).

quiz.q: If τ = 0.5T<sub>s</sub>, find the aperture gain at f<sub>s</sub>/2.
quiz.a: fτ = (f<sub>s</sub>/2)(0.5/f<sub>s</sub>) = 0.25, so the gain is sinc(0.25) ≈ 0.900, about −0.9 dB, against 0.637 for a full-period hold.

beyond: Band-pass sampling is the basis of intermediate-frequency sampling in software-defined radios, where a fast converter digitises a narrow radio band far above zero. At such high input frequencies, random timing errors of the sampling clock (aperture jitter) start to limit the signal-to-noise ratio. Inverse-sinc filters are built into many high-speed DACs. Search next: undersampling, IF sampling, aperture jitter, sinc compensation.

figure.caption: Top: at 2.45 kHz the 5–6 kHz band fits inside zone 5, so its copies fall into the empty gaps and one image lands at 0.1–1.1 kHz the right way round; mirrored copies slope the other way. Bottom: a full-period hold (τ = 125 μs) droops to 0.728 at 3.4 kHz and 0.637 at 4 kHz, while a 10 μs pulse stays almost flat.

spec.aria: Top panel: a band from 5 to 6 kilohertz and its copies between dashed Nyquist zone lines every 1.225 kilohertz, with the image from 0.1 to 1.1 kilohertz highlighted. Bottom panel: sinc gain curves for hold times of 125 and 10 microseconds, with points at 3.4 and 4 kilohertz.
